query:
Please rubber-duck (critique, with sources) the electrical and controls design of a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for aluminium alloy screening (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, 6xxx/7xxx with grain refiners), to be built by a university lab from off-the-shelf parts. The machine: a ~6 L 6061 chamber pumped to ~1 mbar and back-filled with argon at +5 to +20 mbar gauge (O2 < 100 ppm); a 500 W single-mode CW 1070 nm fibre laser (IPG YLR-500-U3, 200-240 VAC single phase, up to 1.7 kW / 1.9 kVA, hardware interlock and analog/gate modulation inputs); a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo on +/-15 V driven over XY2-100 by an RTC6 card in a PC; three Teknic ClearPath-SD integrated servos (recoater, build Z, dosing roller) on 24-75 VDC; a 24 V heated build plate (2-5 x 50 W cartridges in a 6061 block on a piston, control/edge/limit type K thermocouples, a 240 C thermal cutoff, a latching independent limit controller, DC SSR); a rotary-vane pump, a sealed recirculation blower (140-200 L/min at 1.5-3 kPa), solenoid valves, a trace O2 analyzer and dew-point sensor (4-20 mA), pressure transmitters, inductive proximity sensors, a load cell, NFC reader, layer camera; a mechanical safety shutter; guard-locking door interlock, E-stops, key switch, emission lamp; a programmable safety controller (Banner SC26-2 class); an online UPS (1.35 kW) backing the PC, scan head, servos' logic, O2 logging and guard lock; everything on a tray of a vertical lift module, docked to the building's power at one connector, and tended by a UR12e on a mobile base.

Questions: (1) Which electrical standards and practices apply to such a machine in a US university lab (NFPA 79, UL 508A panel practice, NEC Article 670, IEC 60204-1, ISO 13849-1 PL for the laser-enable function, 21 CFR 1040.10 for Class 4, ANSI Z136.1), and what do they require that hobby/lab builds usually miss (disconnecting means, SCCR, overcurrent protection, wire colours and sizes, protective bonding continuity tests, enclosure ratings)? (2) Combustible aluminium powder (NFPA 484, NFPA 652/654, NEC Class II Group E): what electrical classification and practices are needed inside and around the chamber and the filter, and which components must be dust-ignition-proof or intrinsically safe? (3) How should heaters, thermocouples and sensors pass into an argon/vacuum chamber: hermetic multi-pin feedthroughs (KF-flanged), potted PCB feedthroughs, or cable glands; thermocouple-alloy feedthrough pins vs copper pins and cold-junction errors; outgassing of cable insulation (PTFE vs PVC vs silicone vs Kapton) at 200 C. (4) Do lab-built and open-source LPBF machines (for example the ones described in the literature as open-architecture or open-source LPBF/SLM testbeds) use custom PCBs, and for what (galvo XY2-100 interfaces, laser modulation timing, interlock boards, thermocouple boards), or do they use PLCs and DIN-rail modules? What are known failure modes: ground loops between the laser, galvo and PC, EMI from servo drives on thermocouple and analog lines, XY2-100 cable length limits, laser modulation latency and first-pulse effects, galvo supply sequencing? (5) Heated-plate control: PID tuning with laser heat input that exceeds the plate's losses, over-temperature protection architecture (independent limit vs software), SSR derating and failure (SSRs fail shorted). (6) What would you change or add? Please cite sources (papers, standards summaries, vendor application notes, theses on lab-built LPBF machines).
task_summary: Electrical Controls Design Review For Lab-Built LPBF Machine Covering Standards Safety Feedthroughs Failure Modes

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only
        - CASE_CROSSOVER: Case-Crossover
        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population
        - NATURAL_HISTORY: Natural History

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double

    WhoMasked:

        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,

query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

List of disease names to search for.

disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Please rubber-duck (critique, with sources) the electrical and controls design of a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for aluminium alloy screening (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, 6xxx/7xxx with grain refiners), to be built by a university lab from off-the-shelf parts. The machine: a ~6 L 6061 chamber pumped to ~1 mbar and back-filled with argon at +5 to +20 mbar gauge (O2 < 100 ppm); a 500 W single-mode CW 1070 nm fibre laser (IPG YLR-500-U3, 200-240 VAC single phase, up to 1.7 kW / 1.9 kVA, hardware interlock and analog/gate modulation inputs); a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo on +/-15 V driven over XY2-100 by an RTC6 card in a PC; three Teknic ClearPath-SD integrated servos (recoater, build Z, dosing roller) on 24-75 VDC; a 24 V heated build plate (2-5 x 50 W cartridges in a 6061 block on a piston, control/edge/limit type K thermocouples, a 240 C thermal cutoff, a latching independent limit controller, DC SSR); a rotary-vane pump, a sealed recirculation blower (140-200 L/min at 1.5-3 kPa), solenoid valves, a trace O2 analyzer and dew-point sensor (4-20 mA), pressure transmitters, inductive proximity sensors, a load cell, NFC reader, layer camera; a mechanical safety shutter; guard-locking door interlock, E-stops, key switch, emission lamp; a programmable safety controller (Banner SC26-2 class); an online UPS (1.35 kW) backing the PC, scan head, servos' logic, O2 logging and guard lock; everything on a tray of a vertical lift module, docked to the building's power at one connector, and tended by a UR12e on a mobile base.

Questions: (1) Which electrical standards and practices apply to such a machine in a US university lab (NFPA 79, UL 508A panel practice, NEC Article 670, IEC 60204-1, ISO 13849-1 PL for the laser-enable function, 21 CFR 1040.10 for Class 4, ANSI Z136.1), and what do they require that hobby/lab builds usually miss (disconnecting means, SCCR, overcurrent protection, wire colours and sizes, protective bonding continuity tests, enclosure ratings)? (2) Combustible aluminium powder (NFPA 484, NFPA 652/654, NEC Class II Group E): what electrical classification and practices are needed inside and around the chamber and the filter, and which components must be dust-ignition-proof or intrinsically safe? (3) How should heaters, thermocouples and sensors pass into an argon/vacuum chamber: hermetic multi-pin feedthroughs (KF-flanged), potted PCB feedthroughs, or cable glands; thermocouple-alloy feedthrough pins vs copper pins and cold-junction errors; outgassing of cable insulation (PTFE vs PVC vs silicone vs Kapton) at 200 C. (4) Do lab-built and open-source LPBF machines (for example the ones described in the literature as open-architecture or open-source LPBF/SLM testbeds) use custom PCBs, and for what (galvo XY2-100 interfaces, laser modulation timing, interlock boards, thermocouple boards), or do they use PLCs and DIN-rail modules? What are known failure modes: ground loops between the laser, galvo and PC, EMI from servo drives on thermocouple and analog lines, XY2-100 cable length limits, laser modulation latency and first-pulse effects, galvo supply sequencing? (5) Heated-plate control: PID tuning with laser heat input that exceeds the plate's losses, over-temperature protection architecture (independent limit vs software), SSR derating and failure (SSRs fail shorted). (6) What would you change or add? Please cite sources (papers, standards summaries, vendor application notes, theses on lab-built LPBF machines).

Abstract:
<jats:p>Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) has emerged as a leading additive manufacturing (AM) process for producing complex metal components. Despite its advantages, the inherent LPBF process complexity leads to challenges in achieving consistent quality and repeatability. To address these concerns, recent research efforts have focused on sensor fusion techniques for process monitoring, and on developing more elaborate control strategies. Sensor fusion combines information from multiple in situ sensors to provide more comprehensive insights into process characteristics such as melt pool behavior, spatter formation, and layer integrity. By leveraging multimodal data sources, sensor fusion enhances the detection and diagnosis of process anomalies in real-time. Closed-loop control systems may utilize this fused information to adjust key process parameters–such as laser power, focal depth, and scanning speed–to mitigate defect formation during the build process. This review focuses on the current state-of-the-art in sensor fusion monitoring and control strategies for LPBF. In terms of sensor fusion, recent advances extend beyond CNN-based approaches to include graph-based, attention, and transformer architectures. Among these, feature-level integration has shown the best balance between accuracy and computational cost. However, the limited volume of available experimental data, class-imbalance issues and lack of standardization still hinder further progress. In terms of control, a trend away from purely physics-based towards Machine Learning (ML)-assisted and hybrid strategies can be observed. These strategies show promise for more adaptive and effective quality enhancement. The biggest challenge is the broader validation on more complex part geometries and under realistic conditions using commercial LPBF systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Open-loop control of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing (AM) has enabled the production of complex, high-criticality parts for various industries. This method relies on static parameter sets from extensive experimentation and simulations, hoping they remain stable and defect-free in production. Closed-loop control of LPBF can further enhance process stability and reduce defects despite complex thermal histories, process noise, hardware drift, and unexpected perturbations. Controller performance depends on parameter tuning, traditionally a manual, expertise-driven process with no guarantee of optimal performance and limited transferability between systems. This study proposes Bayesian Optimization (BO) to automate in-layer controller tuning by leveraging LPBF's layer-to-layer repetitive nature. Two approaches are introduced: online tuning, adjusting parameters iteratively during the process, and offline tuning, conducted in a setup such as laser exposures on a bare metal plate. These methods are experimentally implemented on an in-layer PI controller, and the performance is investigated on two wedge geometries prone to overheating. Results show that BO effectively tunes controllers using either method, significantly reducing overheating in controlled wedge specimens compared to uncontrolled ones. This study presents the first printed parts controlled by an in-layer controller subjected to microstructural analysis. Findings reveal partial presence of lack-of-fusion porosities due to insufficient laser power assigned by the controller, highlighting a significant challenge for utilizing laser power controllers. In summary, BO presents a promising method for automatic in-layer controller tuning in LPBF, enhancing control precision and mitigating overheating in production parts.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) is increasingly applied for the fabrication of geometric complex components and intricate shapes which are not readily obtained using conventional powder metallurgy processes. Despite the advantages of AM, for many product applications there are challenges related to process-induced defects which can degrade part material properties and reduce its mechanical performance. The incorporation of effective control systems can help to reduce processing defects, improve processing efficiency, and minimize waste. Designing such systems requires careful consideration of the following key factors: 1) defining the control objectives and selecting appropriate controllable inputs, 2) choosing a suitable control category and selecting a relevant control strategy accordingly, 3) developing a mathematical model for model-based control design, and 4) designing a measurement system to acquire data and provide feedback to the controller for processing. Based on these factors, the objective of this paper is to systematically review publications which have reported on the use of control and monitoring systems during metal AM processing. Additionally, this review examines whether control is applied within a single layer or across multiple layers, to provide better insight into deciding between these two control approaches. In addition to the four factors highlighted due to their importance in the design of control systems, a further factor considered in this review is the identification of research gaps and future directions. By examining how these factors were addressed in the literature, this paper aims to identify best control practices for metal AM processing and highlight the potential of less explored areas.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Selective laser melting (SLM), a metal powder fusion additive manufacturing process, has the potential to manufacture complex components for aerospace and biomedical implants. Large-scale adaptation of these technologies is hampered due to the presence of defects such as porosity and part distortion. Nonuniform melt pool size is a major cause of these defects. The melt pool size changes due to heat from the previous powder bed tracks. In this work, the effect of heat sourced from neighbouring tracks was modelled and feedback control was designed. The objective of control is to regulate the melt pool cross-sectional area rejecting the effect of heat from neighbouring tracks within a layer of the powder bed. The SLM process’s thermal model was developed using the energy balance of lumped melt pool volume. The disturbing heat from neighbouring tracks was modelled as the initial temperature of the melt pool. Combining the thermal model with disturbance model resulted in a nonlinear model describing melt pool evolution. The PID, a classical feedback control approach, was used to minimize the effect of intertrack disturbance on the melt pool area. The controller was tuned for the desired melt pool area in a known environment. Simulation results revealed that the proposed controller regulated the desired melt pool area during the scan of multiple tracks of a powder layer within 16 milliseconds and within a length of 0.04 mm reducing laser power by 10% approximately in five tracks. This reduced the chance of pore formation. Hence, it enhances the quality of components manufactured using the SLM process, reducing defects.

Outgassing rates given in the literature, if available, are mostly insufficient to plan and set up a vacuum system, more so if commercial parts, preassembled items, or complex electronics with unknown components are deployed. Outgassing rates have a severe impact on the required pumping speed in ultrahigh vacuum systems and they change if the samples are powered or heated. The newly built apparatus uses the throughput method to measure outgassing rates. It can house probes with a size of [Formula: see text] and supplies electrical currents of up to 5 A. In addition, a heater can establish temperatures of up to 200 [Formula: see text]C directly. A procedure is given to identify the main gas inputs and to retrieve data with a lower limit of [Formula: see text] after 100 h in vacuum. In this paper, we present the experimental setup and first results for samples of polytetrafluorethylene, polyamide (PA6), Viton (1A), and oxygen-free high thermal conductivity copper at room temperature.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As liquid xenon time projection chambers scale to
  ever-larger sizes, so too do the engineering challenges they
  pose. We describe a large, flexible, multipurpose test facility
  capable of supporting the development of a number of key aspects of
  liquid xenon detector systems. Example applications of this facility
  include characterization of large-area light and charge sensor
  arrays, tests of xenon purification techniques and materials
  compatibility, and investigations into high-voltage phenomena. This
  facility uses an automated and remotely monitored cryo-cooling
  system based on immersion of the test chamber in a liquid bath
  rather than conductive coupling, leading to advantages in
  temperature and pressure stability, as well as increasing required
  response times in the case of cooling-power loss. Design advantages,
  operational procedures, and performance of the facility are
  described, as well as five examples of liquid xenon test chambers
  that use the facility.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000004

From text 'buls2018asmartmachine pages 51-54'.

S Buls and JP Kruth. A smart machine for selective laser melting-a controlled & synchronized system approach. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes an open-architecture electrical design for an SLM/LPBF scanning module in which proprietary commercial control electronics are replaced or supplemented by lab-built hardware. The machine uses an in-house, stripped-down RTC-board replacement that retains the main galvo functions while allowing research and advanced control. Its FPGA-based Trajectory Generator calculates intermediate microvectors between commanded coordinates; this replaces the unmodifiable commercial trajectory generator and can later support model-based feedforward control. A separate FPGA XY2-100 Engine packages trajectory coordinates and provides the protocol’s data-link and physical-layer functions. The custom Scanner Interface Board converts low-voltage, single-ended FPGA outputs for CLOCK, SYNC, CHANX, and CHANY into the ±15 V differential signaling required by the galvo scanner. The interface circuitry is based on an LTC487CSW RS485 driver, with differential line pairs and termination shown in the design. The broader architecture synchronizes the laser and galvo scanner as one process-specific system rather than treating them as independent generic black-box components. This excerpt does not provide implementation details for laser modulation, interlock or thermocouple PCBs, nor does it report failure modes such as ground loops, servo-drive EMI, XY2-100 cable faults, laser first-pulse effects, or galvo power-supply sequencing.

## pqac-00000005

From text 'buls2018asmartmachine pages 54-56'.

S Buls and JP Kruth. A smart machine for selective laser melting-a controlled & synchronized system approach. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes an open, modular electrical architecture for controlling and monitoring a galvo-based SLM machine. A Position Measurement Block acquires signals from buffered encoder probes, using simultaneous sampling at rates up to 20 kHz and synchronizing position data with other process measurements, including laser power, base-plate temperature, and chamber pressure. A separate Position Estimator Block can simulate actual galvo-mirror positions from commanded trajectories and a physical scanner model, providing a non-invasive alternative to encoder probing. The system overview places a PXI/FPGA controller between the trajectory generator and an XY2-100 scanner interface board, which converts single-ended signals to differential signals for the galvo scanner and interfaces with the XY2-100 protocol. The excerpt also emphasizes laser-source power stability: fluctuations directly affect the melt pool and can introduce unpredictable variance or noise into melt-pool monitoring. It identifies fiber lasers as the preferred source for metallic SLM because of their beam quality and efficiency. However, these pages do not provide implementation details for custom laser-modulation, interlock, thermocouple, or power-supply sequencing boards, nor do they document failure modes such as ground loops, servo-drive EMI, XY2-100 cable faults, first-pulse laser effects, or galvo supply sequencing.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'buls2018asmartmachinea pages 51-54'.

S Buls and JP Kruth. A smart machine for selective laser melting-a controlled & synchronized system approach. Unknown journal, 2018.

The excerpt describes an electrically open, lab-built replacement for the proprietary SCANLAB RTC interface used with a HurryScan25 galvo scanner. The custom design is an in-house stripped-down RTC board implemented around FPGA logic and retains the principal galvo functions while allowing research and advanced control development. Its main blocks include a trajectory generator, an XY2-100 engine, and a scanner interface board. The trajectory generator computes intermediate position points (microvectors) between start and end coordinates, replacing the commercial linear-interpolation implementation and providing a basis for model-based feedforward control. The XY2-100 engine implements the data-link and physical-layer functions needed to package and transmit generated coordinates to the scanner. The scanner interface converts low-voltage, single-ended FPGA signals into the ±15 V differential signals required by the XY2-100 standard, including clock, synchronization, X-channel, and Y-channel lines. The interface circuitry is based on an LTC487CSW RS485 driver. The excerpt also explains the motivation for coordinated control: factory-tuned black-box laser and scanner controllers may produce generic dynamics that are unsuitable for SLM, potentially destabilizing the melt pool and reducing part quality. It does not provide information about laser-modulation PCBs, interlock boards, thermocouple boards, ground loops, EMI from servo drives, XY2-100 cable failures, first-pulse laser effects, or galvo power-supply sequencing.

This article has 19 citations.

The excerpt describes the electrical and data-acquisition architecture of an open-protocol SLM research platform, but it does not provide detailed schematics for custom PCBs, interlock boards, thermocouple boards, or specific failure modes. The system separates real-time, high-speed signals from slower machine-monitoring data. High-speed data, operating at approximately 100 kHz, use a digital protocol similar to XY2-100 for synchronous transmission of signals such as laser and scanner-related measurements. Lower-speed data, typically 1–10 Hz, use an Ethernet-based, MTConnect-like protocol for machine and management information. A real-time DAQ system interfaces heterogeneous sensors, including sensors producing analog voltages, while a Windows-based host PC handles low-speed sensors and data storage. Both streams are buffered, synchronized through network-shared variables using a 10 Hz sampling loop, and saved locally or on a network. Abstract:
The growing trend towards high voltage electrical assets and propulsion in the aeronautics and space industry pose new challenges in electrical insulation materials that cannot be overlooked. Transition to new high voltage electrified systems with unprecedented high levels of voltage, power, and efficiency must be safe and reliable. Improvements in both performance and safety of megawatt power systems is complicated because of the need for additional power transmission wiring and cabling and new safety requirements that have the potential of making the resulting systems heavier. To mitigate this issue, novel lightweight materials and system solutions are required that would result in lower specific weights in the insulator and conductor. Although reduced size and weight of system components can be achieved with new concepts, designs, and technologies, the high voltage (≥300 V) operation presents a significant challenge. This challenge is further complicated when considering the extreme operating environment that is experienced in aircraft, spacecraft, and targeted human exploration destinations. This paper reviews the extreme environmental challenges for aerospace electrical insulation and the needs associated with operating under high voltage and extreme environments. It also examines several recently developed robust lightweight electrical insulation materials that could enhance insulation performance and life. In aerospace, research must consider mass when developing new technologies. The impact of these recent developments provides a pathway which could enable next generation high altitude all electric aircraft, lightweight power transmission cables for a future sustained presence on the Moon and missions to Mars using HV propulsion, such as spacecraft with Nuclear Electric Propulsion systems.

                    This journal,

                    , celebrates its 10th anniversary in 2026. To commemorate this significant milestone, this comprehensive special review article showcases the latest global research progress and cutting‐edge advancements in polymeric insulating materials, a critical component that underpins high‐voltage systems and is vital to modern infrastructure. The analysis of the literature on polymer insulating materials produced over the period from around the world was conducted by 11 researchers and presented on a regional basis. Distinctive research can be highlighted in different places, such as materials for power generation and transmission in the Nordic region, charge transport and space charge in France, molecular design in China, and revitalised current integration methods in Japan. The survey reveals that research on winding insulation in rotating machines has been highly active over the past decade due to advancements in power electronics. Particularly notable is the attention given to partial discharges under low pressure related to the development of electric aircraft. Additionally, solid insulation in cables and other components of high‐voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission systems and other emerging themes, such as green, lower‐carbon insulation, have attracted interest. Materials such as polypropylene‐based blends for HVDC applications, multilayers in aeronautic cables and polyimide‐based nanocomposites for windings and power module packaging have been particularly investigated. The importance of research using computer‐aided methods, such as numerical analysis, computational science, materials informatics, neural networks, and machine learning, has been steadily growing.

Abstract:
Newly developed multilayer structures of well-known polymer insulation materials significantly improved dielectric breakdown voltage, VB, or dielectric strength, K, if well-bonded, when compared to those of single material insulations or the commercial SOA systems, such as Teflon-Kapton-Teflon (TKT), at the same overall thickness. To date, the greatest improvement of the new structures from a few candidate materials, including various types of Kapton PIs and PFA or PET as bond layer (BL), was about 61% higher than that of the Kapton PI alone films, 40.1 vs. 24.9 kV, which was translated to 86.3% decrease in insulation thickness, thus significant volume and weight reduction of the final system. However, it was of interest to note that most improvements of the multilayer structures occurred at thicker overall thicknesses, above ~ 0.15 mm. Extensive analyses also showed that K of the multilayer structures increased with (i) decreasing individual layer thickness regardless of material type, (ii) increasing total accumulated thickness of PI or overall PI/BL ratio, and (iii) increasing number of interface or total number of layers, but only above the aforementioned overall thickness limit. Increases in VB or K of the multilayer structures were directly correlated with damage evolution and failure mode. With further material-design-process optimizations of the multilayer structures, it was expected to achieve other multifunctionalities, such as high partial discharge (PD) resistance, improved durability, EMI shielding, and high thermal dissipation in addition to high dielectric strength. These new structures can be used in various high voltage and high temperature applications, such as future hybrid or all electric aircraft wiring and power transmission as well as many other non-aerospace high power cables, electronic parts and components, printed circuit board, and so forth. The multilayer insulation system can be easily processed and manufactured with various conductor types via calendaring, compression-molding, stamping, laminating, vacuum-bagging and autoclaving, or 3D printing, even for complex 3-D components. Based on their unique structural configurations and potential capabilities, the new insulation system was identified as micro-multilayer multifunctional electrical insulation (MMEI). Patent application of the MMEI concept and current design configurations was filed for a 1-year provisional application (OAI-58834, Serial No.: 62/659,234), pending conversion to a U.S. utility application. This paper presents details of the MMEI structures, their dielectric performance analyses, potential mechanisms, and commercial scaleup feasibility assessment.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) is an additive manufacturing technology that is gaining increasing interest in aerospace, automotive and biomedical applications due to the possibility of processing lightweight alloys such as AlSi10Mg and Ti6Al4V. Both these alloys have microstructures and mechanical properties that are strictly related to the type of heat treatment applied after the L-PBF process. The present review aimed to summarize the state of the art in terms of the microstructural morphology and consequent mechanical performance of these materials after different heat treatments. While optimization of the post-process heat treatment is key to obtaining excellent mechanical properties, the first requirement is to manufacture high quality and fully dense samples. Therefore, effects induced by the L-PBF process parameters and build platform temperatures were also summarized. In addition, effects induced by stress relief, annealing, solution, artificial and direct aging, hot isostatic pressing, and mixed heat treatments were reviewed for AlSi10Mg and Ti6AlV samples, highlighting variations in microstructure and corrosion resistance and consequent fracture mechanisms.

Abstract:
AlSi10Mg alloy is mainly produced by laser fusion on a powder bed. It offers a good compromise between easy processing and good mechanical properties. These properties depend on the manufacturing parameters, including the preheating temperature, as this alloy hardens by precipitation. This study explored the effect of preheating to 170 °C on the mechanical properties and microstructure of this alloy as a function of the manufacturing time. The mechanical properties were characterized by tensile, hardness and impact strength tests as a function of the sample height. An anisotropic behavior was confirmed: the horizontal orientation showed higher deformation and fracture energies. In addition, a gradient of properties appeared as a function of the distance from the platform; the closer the sample was to the platform, the higher its fracture energy and the lower its hardness. The hardness values followed the same evolution as a function of the distance to the platform as that of the hardness curve after ageing post-treatment. It was therefore shown that the preheating of the platform generated in situ ageing with respect to the manufacturing height: a hardness peak was obtained at a certain distance from the plateau (40 mm—10 h of remaining manufacturing time) and over-aging near the plateau was induced by long exposure times at 170 °C.

Abstract:
Few systematic studies on the correlation between alloy microstructure and mechanical failure of the AlSi10Mg alloy produced by laser-based powder bed fusion (L-PBF) are available in the literature. This work investigates the fracture mechanisms of the L-PBF AlSi10Mg alloy in as-built (AB) condition and after three different heat treatments (T5 (4 h at 160 °C), standard T6 (T6B) (1 h at 540 °C followed by 4 h at 160 °C), and rapid T6 (T6R) (10 min at 510 °C followed by 6 h at 160 °C)). In-situ tensile tests were conducted with scanning electron microscopy combined with electron backscattering diffraction. In all samples the crack nucleation was at defects. In AB and T5, the interconnected Si network fostered damage at low strain due to the formation of voids and the fragmentation of the Si phase. T6 heat treatment (T6B and T6R) formed a discrete globular Si morphology with less stress concentration, which delayed the void nucleation and growth in the Al matrix. The analysis empirically confirmed the higher ductility of the T6 microstructure than that of the AB and T5, highlighting the positive effects on the mechanical performance of the more homogeneous distribution of finer Si particles in T6R.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The influence of base plate temperature (25, 100, 200, and 400 °C) on the laser powder bed fusion processing of EN AW 7075 was systematically investigated using microstructural characterisation (LM, SEM, EBSD, GROD), chemical analysis, hardness testing, and thermal simulations across a broad range of process parameters. Moderate preheating at 100 °C and 200 °C showed no significant reduction in crack density or changes in grain morphology compared to processing without preheating. At the highest studied temperature—400 °C—a transition to columnar crack networks was observed, accompanied by modified grain orientation, pronounced stress relaxation, and reduced hardness. Independent of preheating temperature, consistent evaporation of Zn (~1 wt.%) and Mg (~0.3 wt.%) occurred during processing. Thermal simulations qualitatively supported the experimental observations, indicating increased thermal retention and displacement with increasing preheating temperature. The results demonstrate that base plate preheating alone is insufficient to suppress hot cracking in EN AW 7075 and may promote alternative crack-growth mechanisms at elevated temperatures, highlighting the need for alternative alloy or process design strategies.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Mise en œuvre d'un alliage d'aluminium structural par fusion laser sur lit de poudres : étude des mécanismes de fissuration</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">Dans cette thèse, une analyse de la sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud en fonction (i) des paramètres de premier ordre (puissance, vitesse) du procédé de fusion laser sur lit de poudres (L-PBF : Laser Powder Bed Fusion) et (ii) de la variation de la teneur en soluté (Si et Mg principalement) est présentée pour l'alliage d'aluminium à durcissement structural 6061 (Al-0.8Si-1.2Mg wt%). Le mécanisme de fissuration à chaud est identifié comme une fissuration par solidification sur la base d'observations expérimentales des microstructures. En accord avec des travaux antérieurs publiés sur d’autres familles d’alliages, les fissures se propagent aux joints de grains de fortes désorientations et sont préférentiellement situées au centre des bains de fusion. En utilisant le critère de Rappaz-Drezet-Gremaud (RDG criterion) combiné à des simulations thermiques utilisant le formalisme de Rosenthal, la localisation des fissures correspond aux régions des bains de fusion ou la sollicitation mécanique intergranulaire est la plus élevée lors de la solidification. Des cartes de sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud sont ensuite développées pour prédire de manière simple les variations de sensibilité à la fissuration à chaud en fonction des paramètres du procédé de premier ordre, à savoir la puissance laser et la vitesse de balayage ainsi que des conditions de préchauffage. Les tendances prédites sont qualitativement en accord avec les observations expérimentales. Les résultats permettent de discuter de l'impact des conditions d’élaboration sur la réduction de la fissuration à chaud et également d’identifier les paramètres métallurgiques clés de ce mécanisme de fissuration.</jats:p>

                                                     ix    Chapter 1: Introduction

1.1: THE SLS PROCESS

       Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) is a powder fusion based additive manufacturing process

which was developed at the University of Texas at Austin. As the name suggests, a laser is used

to selectively heat portions of a flat powder bed, ‘sintering’ or melting the powder together to

create a desired two-dimensional shape. This shape corresponds to a single cross-section of a three-

dimensional part. By stacking multiple cross-sections together, a three-dimensional part is formed.


       In SLS, similar to other additive manufacturing techniques, a 3D model is sliced into two

dimensional layers, which are then sliced into a series of lines, or vectors, which represent laser

scan paths. The process begins with a build chamber which is partially full of powder. This build

chamber is heated to a preset temperature below the melting point of the material being used. Next,

a roller is used to spread a thin, even layer of powder across the top of the build chamber. The laser

is then used to selectively melt a portion of the powder layer corresponding to a 2D cross sectional

area of the final part. The roller then spreads a new layer and the process is repeated for each 2D

cross section until the full three dimensional part is built.





                                          1         Figure 1: Selective Laser Sintering Process (Carpenter, 2014)


1.2: Experimental Motivation

       Previous work has shown that the quality of a part built using Selective Laser Sintering is

highly affected by the temperature control of the part during the build (Benda, 1994) (Wroe, et al.,

2016). More specifically, the maximum temperature of each particle of powder during the laser

melting process is critical to achieving a high quality part. If the maximum temperature is too low,

the powder does not fully melt, resulting in a poor bond and a structural weakness. Conversely, if

the maximum temperature is too high, over sintering occurs which can cause part growth and

dimensional inaccuracies. The maximum temperature of the powder is influenced by the pre-

sintering temperature of the powder and the amount of energy deposited by the laser. Theoretically,

the powder bed can be heated to a uniform temperature just below the melting temperature and a

constant laser power can then be used to further heat the powder to the optimal temperature.




                                          2     To achieve this thermally uniform powder bed, SLS machines can have an insulated build

chamber which is heated with a series of radiant heaters. These heaters can be placed strategically

throughout the machine to create a uniform temperature, however geometrical limitations of the

build chamber can limit their effectiveness. A typical commercial machine has a temperature

gradient of 10-15 degrees Celsius across the powder bed (Hall, 2015) (Bourell, Watt, Leigh, &

Fulcher, 2014). Additionally, during a build new variations in temperature across the powder bed

surface can develop due to the presence of previously sintered layers underneath the freshly spread

powder layer (Phillips, 2016).





         Figure 2: Build Surface Temperature Gradient (Bourell, Watt, Leigh, & Fulcher, 2014)


       Previous work has shown that if a temperature gradient exists in the pre-sintered powder

bed, this gradient will also be reflected in the maximum temperature of the powder during the

sintering process if a constant laser power is used (Phillips, 2016). Figure 3 shows the results of

this work, illustrating that if the pre-sintering temperatures are shifted up by adding a constant to

them, they match the post-sintering temperatures extremely well. This thermal gradient, preserved

in the post-sintering temperatures, will lead to regions of un-melted and over sintered powder,

leading to structural weakness or part deformity as described above.

                                          3         Figure 3: Pre-Sintering and Post-Sintering Temperatures Along a Scan Line (Phillips, 2016)


       Since it is difficult to create a fully thermally uniform powder bed, another option is to vary

laser power across the powder bed. By varying laser power inversely with respect to pre-sintered

temperature, the goal of a uniform (and optimal) maximum temperature can be achieved. Previous

work at The University of Austin at Texas has verified that this is a viable solution to the problem

of a temperature gradient (Phillips, 2016). However, limitations in current off-the-shelf laser

scanning systems makes implementation difficult. Current commercial laser scanning systems do

not allow the laser power to be varied across the length of a single scan line. In previous

experiments, a single scan line was divided into multiple smaller scan lines which were each given

a constant power. Although this method is effective in reducing the post-sintering temperature

gradient, dividing a single scan line into multiple smaller scan lines can cause addition problems

with uneven heating of the powder bed. At the beginning and end of each scan line, there is an



                                          4acceleration region due to the inertia of the galvanometers. If a constant laser power is used during

this acceleration region, more energy is deposited per unit area at the lower velocity, leading to an

increase in temperature of that area. A more complete solution is to continuously vary the power

across the entire scan line, allowing the post-sintering gradient to be reduced without creating

additional hot-spots due to acceleration regions. This paper reviews the design and implementation

of a modified laser scan system which allows the laser power to be varied across a scan line based

on the position of the galvanometers. Although the scan system was only tested for polymer

powders, it should be equally beneficial for SLS of any material.

5.

## pqac-00000026

From text 'bosio2021productionstrategyfor pages 1-2'.

Federico Bosio, Haopeng Shen, Yang Liu, Mariangela Lombardi, Paul Rometsch, Xinhua Wu, Yuman Zhu, and Aijun Huang. Production strategy for manufacturing large-scale alsi10mg components by laser powder bed fusion. JOM, 73:770-780, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-020-04523-8, doi:10.1007/s11837-020-04523-8. This article has 42 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt directly reports that constant build-platform temperatures of 150°C and 200°C were effective for large-scale AlSi10Mg LPBF: they prevented cracking and minimized distortion. The proposed mechanism is reduction of thermal gradients, residual stresses, and solidification shrinkage when the plate is heated throughout the build. The excerpt does not provide results for 100°C, 170°C, or 400°C, so no conclusions about those temperatures can be drawn from this passage. Related studies cited in the introduction used 160°C for AlSi10Mg and 80°C or 250°C for related aluminum alloys. Heating also changes microstructure through in-situ aging. In Al-Si alloys, platform heating can promote precipitation, including Mg2Si precipitates in A357 and nanoscale Si particles in AlSi10Mg/A357-type material. These changes may increase hardness under suitable conditions, but excessive holding at temperature can cause over-aging and lower hardness. In the reported work, samples at 150°C reached peak hardness with less than 13 hours of holding; holding longer than 13 hours at 150°C or 200°C produced obvious over-aging. The resulting hardness loss could be recovered using a T6 post-process heat treatment.


---

## pqac-00000027

From text 'chambrin2022insituageing pages 1-2'.

Nicolas Chambrin, Olivier Dalverny, Jean-Marc Cloue, Olivier Brucelle, and Joel Alexis. In situ ageing with the platform preheating of alsi10mg alloy manufactured by laser powder-bed fusion process. Metals, 12:2148, Dec 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met12122148, doi:10.3390/met12122148. This article has 14 citations.

The excerpt directly documents LPBF platform preheating at 170 °C and 200 °C, and reports that precipitation can be induced by in situ ageing at temperatures above 140 °C. It does not provide specific evidence for 100 °C, 150 °C, or 400 °C, so those temperatures cannot be characterized from this excerpt. Heated plates were initially used to reduce thermal stresses and help prevent hot cracking, which is particularly relevant for difficult-to-process aluminium alloys. However, preheating also changes the AlSi10Mg microstructure and hardening response. At temperatures above approximately 140 °C, in situ precipitation occurs during the build. At 200 °C, Si precipitation inside the Al cellular regions is reported together with reduced yield strength. The detailed 170 °C study found that prolonged exposure produces a height-dependent ageing gradient: material closer to the platform experiences longer heating, lower hardness, and higher fracture energy, while a hardness peak occurs farther from the platform; over-ageing near the platform is attributed to long exposure at 170 °C. The as-built alloy consists of a fine Al cellular phase surrounded by a Si-rich eutectic phase, and platform heating modifies this metastable structure through diffusion-controlled precipitation.


---

## pqac-00000028

From text 'velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 2-4'.

Nejc Velikajne, Jožef Medved, Črtomir Donik, and Irena Paulin. Influence of base plate preheating on laser powder bed fusion–processed en aw-7075 aluminium alloy. Materials, 19:970, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma19050970, doi:10.3390/ma19050970. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt reports LPBF experiments and simulations on EN AW 7075 aluminium using build-plate temperatures of 25, 100, 200, and 400 °C. Thus, it directly documents 100, 200, and 400 °C, but it does not provide evidence for 150 or 170 °C. The study’s central hypothesis is that heating the plate reduces thermal gradients and solidification stresses, which should lower hot-cracking susceptibility. Elevated preheating can also reduce porosity and cracking, while changing thermal retention, distortion, and stress evolution. However, heating does not necessarily produce crack-free builds across practical processing windows. Its effects may depend on microsegregation, crack propagation, melt-pool lifetime, segregation behaviour, and stress relaxation; sufficiently high preheating may therefore become ineffective or detrimental and enable alternative crack-growth pathways. The research specifically seeks to connect preheating with Zn/Mg chemical stability, crack morphology, grain-structure evolution, local lattice misorientation/internal strain measured by EBSD-based GROD, and hardness. Thermo-mechanical simulations were used to compare temperature distributions and displacement as preheating increased. The excerpt therefore supports a temperature-dependent trade-off: moderate or elevated heating can mitigate thermal-stress-driven cracking, but may alter microstructure and segregation-related mechanisms in ways that prevent universal crack suppression.


---

## pqac-00000029

From text 'velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 1-2'.

Nejc Velikajne, Jožef Medved, Črtomir Donik, and Irena Paulin. Influence of base plate preheating on laser powder bed fusion–processed en aw-7075 aluminium alloy. Materials, 19:970, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma19050970, doi:10.3390/ma19050970. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt reports LPBF experiments on EN AW-7075 aluminium using base-plate temperatures of 25 °C (no preheating), 100 °C, 200 °C, and 400 °C. It does not provide results for 150 °C or 170 °C. Preheating to 100 °C and 200 °C produced no significant reduction in crack density and no notable change in grain morphology compared with room-temperature processing. At 400 °C, the cracking behavior changed rather than being eliminated: the material developed columnar crack networks, with modified grain orientation, pronounced stress relaxation, and lower hardness. Thermal simulations indicated greater thermal retention and displacement as the preheating temperature increased. The introduction explains that preheating can reduce thermal gradients, slow cooling, and potentially reduce residual stress, but for EN AW-7075 the results show that this thermal approach alone does not suppress hot cracking. The alloy’s intrinsic susceptibility is linked to its wide solidification range, microsegregation, limited interdendritic feeding, and columnar grain growth. The excerpt suggests that elevated preheating may promote alternative crack-growth mechanisms, while alloy/feedstock modification and grain refinement are more promising routes for reducing cracking.


---

## pqac-00000030

From text 'velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 8-11'.

Nejc Velikajne, Jožef Medved, Črtomir Donik, and Irena Paulin. Influence of base plate preheating on laser powder bed fusion–processed en aw-7075 aluminium alloy. Materials, 19:970, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma19050970, doi:10.3390/ma19050970. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt directly evaluates LPBF build-plate temperatures of 25 °C (no preheating), 100 °C, 200 °C, and 400 °C; it does not provide results for 150 °C or 170 °C. Preheating to 100 °C produced the highest hardness and retained much of the LPBF-induced strain hardening, while 200 °C caused only a modest hardness reduction. Neither 100 °C nor 200 °C substantially changed the grain structure, crack morphology, or crack density compared with the unheated condition. Thus, moderate plate heating reduced thermal gradients but was insufficient to suppress the intrinsic hot-cracking susceptibility of EN AW 7075, which is associated with its wide solidification range, microsegregation, and rapid solidification. At 400 °C, the material response changed markedly: strong thermal retention, increased displacement, recovery, and stress relaxation reduced hardness and internal stress. The high temperature promoted segregation of low-melting Zn–Mg–Cu-rich phases and grain-boundary weakening, producing distinct columnar crack networks and facilitating crack propagation along the build direction. Therefore, the excerpt supports 100 °C as beneficial for hardness, 200 °C as largely ineffective for crack elimination, and 400 °C as detrimental because it changes the cracking mechanism and weakens the microstructure.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'velikajne2026influenceofbase pages 6-8'.

Nejc Velikajne, Jožef Medved, Črtomir Donik, and Irena Paulin. Influence of base plate preheating on laser powder bed fusion–processed en aw-7075 aluminium alloy. Materials, 19:970, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma19050970, doi:10.3390/ma19050970. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt directly evaluates LPBF base-plate preheating at room temperature (25°C), 100°C, 200°C, and 400°C for EN AW 7075 aluminium alloy. It does not provide data for 150°C or 170°C, so those temperatures cannot be assessed from this source. Hot cracks were prominent in the printed cross-sections. Increasing the base-plate temperature was proposed as a way to reduce cooling speed and thereby mitigate cracking, but the response was temperature-dependent. At 100°C and 200°C, the microstructures were broadly comparable to those produced without preheating, and EBSD showed minimal-to-no effect on grain size, morphology, internal stresses, or distribution. The 400°C condition produced a clear microstructural change: columnar cracks appeared, and smaller grains showed a different orientation along the build direction. GROD analysis found lower local strain at 100°C than at 200°C, while the 400°C samples had lower dislocation density, suggesting thermal relaxation at sufficiently high preheating temperatures. Thus, moderate preheating may alter cracking conditions without substantially changing grain structure, whereas 400°C significantly changes microstructure and crack morphology.


---

## pqac-00000032

From text 'bosio2021productionstrategyfor pages 2-4'.

Federico Bosio, Haopeng Shen, Yang Liu, Mariangela Lombardi, Paul Rometsch, Xinhua Wu, Yuman Zhu, and Aijun Huang. Production strategy for manufacturing large-scale alsi10mg components by laser powder bed fusion. JOM, 73:770-780, Jan 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-020-04523-8, doi:10.1007/s11837-020-04523-8. This article has 42 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt evaluates LPBF platform temperatures of room temperature (45°C), 100°C, 150°C, and 200°C for AlSi10Mg; it does not provide evidence here for 170°C or 400°C. At 45°C and 100°C, cracks and support distortions occur, particularly in the first consolidated layers between the supports and cantilever arms. Heating the platform to 150°C or 200°C significantly reduces these defects, consistent with alleviation of macro-residual stresses. The heated plate also acts as an in-situ aging treatment during the long build. The aging response depends on both the holding time and the position along the build direction because lower layers remain exposed to the heated platform longer. At 150°C, a maximum printing-time limit is needed to avoid in-situ over-aging. At 200°C, over-aging can occur during printing; however, a subsequent T6-like treatment (solution treatment, quenching, and artificial aging) can increase hardness. The excerpt therefore links preheating to reduced hot-cracking/distortion risk and to microstructural evolution through time- and position-dependent age hardening and over-aging.
